docs.title: Rust core
docs.text:
Hot-path operations (flattening, merging, diffing, hashing) are implemented in Rust and exposed to Python via PyO3. Pure-Python fallbacks activate automatically if the Rust extension is not compiled — so the service always works, just slightly slower without it.

Module Purpose flatten BFS / DFS nested dict → flat key.subkey map merge Variable map overlay + environment resolution sync BLAKE3 content hash for GIT_SMART_REPAIR

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Destination template — control where data lands per rule
  • Environment resolution — map branches, PRs, and tags to environments
  • Sync strategies — choose how writes are applied
  • Drift detection — how the watcher catches and heals config drift

docs.title: Destination Template
docs.text: destination_template is a rule-level field that controls exactly where data lands in each sink — the collection name, key prefix, znode path, file path, or release name — using placeholders resolved at sync time.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text: Placeholder Resolved from {env} Resolved environment (e.g. production, staging, pr-42) {tenant} The tenant the rule belongs to: the tenant whose bundle.json layers it, or the repository owner when the rule names none

docs.title: Per-sink behavior
docs.text: Sink What it controls Template Resolved value MongoDB Collection name "{env}-config" production-config ZooKeeper znode root path "/{tenant}/{env}" /acme/pr-42 Redis Key prefix "{env}:cfg" production:cfg S3 Key prefix "{tenant}/{env}/" acme/production/ Linux server Full remote file path "/etc/app/{env}.env" /etc/app/production.env Helm Release name "app-{env}" app-production ConfigMap ConfigMap name "myapp-{env}" myapp-production Vercel Environment variable prefix "{env}_" production_

docs.title: One template, three environments
docs.text:
rules: [{
  platform:             "github"
  datasource:           "mongo"
  file_name:            "configs/app.yaml"
  repositories:         ["my-org/*"]
  destination_template: "{env}-config"
  branch_map: {
    main:    "production"
    develop: "staging"
    test:    "test"
  }
}]
Push branch Resolved env Collection written to main production production-config develop staging staging-config test test test-config

docs.title: Per-tenant isolation
docs.text:
destination_template: "{tenant}/{env}-config"

A push from tenant acme to main writes to acme/production-config. A push from tenant globex to main writes to globex/production-config.

docs.title: PR preview environments
docs.text:
rules: [{
  platform:             "github"
  datasource:           "mongo"
  file_name:            "configs/app.yaml"
  repositories:         ["my-org/app"]
  destination_template: "{env}-config"
  pr_as_env:            true    // PR #42 → env = "pr-42"
}]

Each pull request gets its own isolated collection: pr-42-config, pr-103-config, etc.

docs.title: ZooKeeper path per tenant and environment
docs.text:
rules: [{
  platform:             "github"
  datasource:           "zookeeper"
  destination_template: "/{tenant}/{env}"
}]

Writes znodes under /acme/production/, /acme/staging/, etc.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
If {env} appears in the template, at least one environment resolution strategy must be enabled:

  • branch_as_env: true
  • pr_as_env: true
  • tag_as_env: true
  • branch_map: { ... }
  • file_path_map: { ... }

varTrack will reject the bundle at startup if {env} is used with no resolution strategy configured.

docs.title: Fallback behavior
docs.text: If destination_template is not set, each sink falls back to its own sink-specific configuration key (e.g. collection for MongoDB, key_prefix for Redis).

docs.title: Drift Detection & Self-Heal
docs.text: For every rule with self_heal: true, the watcher-service asks the orchestrator on each poll whether the datasource still matches Git, and has it restore the ones that don't.

docs.title: What is drift?
docs.text:
Drift happens when a datasource value no longer matches what Git says it should be. Common causes:

  • A developer edits MongoDB directly during an incident
  • A deployment script overwrites a config value
  • A Kubernetes operator changes a ConfigMap
  • A Redis key expires or is flushed

Without drift detection, these changes go unnoticed until something breaks.

docs.title: How detection works
docs.text:
The orchestrator is the one component that reads and writes the sinks: it holds their credentials and their client code. So it also does the comparing. On every poll the watcher calls CheckDatasource; the orchestrator reads, in each synced environment, the keys varTrack wrote and compares them with what it last synced from Git (the sync ledger). The watcher itself reads no sink and holds no sink credentials.

Every POLL_INTERVAL (default: 60s), for each self_heal rule
  │
  └── CheckDatasource → the orchestrator reads the sink, key by key
        ├── in sync  → nothing to do
        ├── syncing  → a sync is still writing: look again on the next poll
        ├── unknown  → can't tell (never synced, sink unreadable): no heal
        └── drifted  → vartrack_watcher_drift_detected_total + 1
              └── Heal: SyncDatasource → the orchestrator re-syncs this
                  datasource from the head of every branch that feeds it

A few rules keep this from healing what it shouldn't, or waiting forever:

  • Unknown is not drift. A sink that cannot be read answers unknown, never "every key is missing", so an outage does not set off heals. A value the sink never gives back — a Vercel sensitive variable — is neither missing nor changed.
  • One heal at a time. After it asks for a heal, the watcher waits two poll intervals (at least 30 s) before asking again for the same drift, so the queued sync has time to start; a check that answers in sync ends the wait.
  • A failed heal is tried again on the next poll; while heal requests keep failing, a circuit breaker stops sending them for a while.
  • A sync that died — a worker killed mid-sync leaves no result. A sync still marked running after 15 minutes (Celery stops any task after 10) no longer counts, so the watcher heals instead of waiting on it.

docs.title: Enabling self-heal
docs.text:
Set self_heal: true on a rule to enable automatic repair:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  self_heal:  true    // watcher will restore state on drift
}]

The watcher asks the orchestrator which rules to watch on every poll, so a rule that gains self_heal, or is suspended or removed, is picked up at the next poll, without restarting the watcher. Rules with self_heal: false (or omitted) are not polled by the watcher, and nothing repairs them. The web UI still compares them with Git whenever it reads them, so their drift shows there until someone syncs from Git:

docs.title: Concrete example
docs.text:
Your config in Git:

max_connections: 50
log_level: info

Someone runs db.variables.updateOne({key: "max_connections"}, {$set: {value: 5}}) directly in MongoDB.

On the next poll cycle:

  1. The watcher asks the orchestrator (CheckDatasource): Git says 50, MongoDB has 5 — drifted
  2. self_heal: true → it calls SyncDatasource on the orchestrator
  3. The orchestrator fetches the file from Git, parses it, writes max_connections = 50 back to MongoDB
  4. The next check answers in sync — state restored

Had the change come from a push to Git, the sync of that push would have recorded it, step 1 would have answered in sync, and nothing would be healed.

Total recovery time: up to one POLL_INTERVAL (default 60 seconds).

On the web UI's Events page a repair shows as Healed. Drift on rules without self-heal shows as Drift detected and stays until someone syncs:

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Monitor drift in Prometheus / Grafana:

Metric Type Description vartrack_watcher_drift_detected_total Counter Drift found, by rule vartrack_watcher_heal_triggered_total Counter Heals the orchestrator accepted vartrack_watcher_heal_failed_total Counter Heals that could not be requested vartrack_watcher_poll_duration_seconds Histogram How long a CheckDatasource took vartrack_watcher_up Gauge 1 while a rule's loop runs

docs.title: Poll interval
docs.text:
Adjust how often the watcher checks each datasource:

POLL_INTERVAL=30s go run ./watcher-service/cmd

Lower values mean faster drift detection but more load on the orchestrator, which reads every self-heal datasource each poll.

docs.title: Why polling? (and how it's kept efficient)
docs.text:
varTrack uses a scheduled pull model rather than event-driven push because it must support eight fundamentally different backends — MongoDB, Redis, ZooKeeper, S3, Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Helm, Vercel, and Linux servers. Each backend exposes a different (or no) change-notification mechanism:

Datasource Native change events? MongoDB Change Streams (replica set only) Redis Keyspace notifications (off by default, extra config) ZooKeeper Watches (per-znode, limited concurrency) S3 Event notifications (requires SNS/SQS wiring) Linux server None — SSH file stat only Vercel None ConfigMap Kubernetes informer (requires in-cluster) Helm None — release state only

A unified polling model means a single code path works across all backends with no external infrastructure requirements.

How the overhead is minimised:

  • Lightweight reads — the orchestrator reads only the keys varTrack wrote in each environment, not the entire datasource, and reads the environments of a datasource in parallel.
  • Configurable interval — default 60 s; set POLL_INTERVAL to match your SLA.
  • Leader election — in multi-replica deployments, only one replica polls (ZooKeeper or Redis distributed lock).
  • Circuit breaker — while heal requests keep failing, the watcher stops sending them for a while.

docs.title: Multi-replica deployments
docs.text:
When running multiple watcher replicas, only one should poll and heal at a time. Leader election ensures this:

bundle: {
  watcher_leader_election_datasource: "redis"   // or "zookeeper"
}

This is the only thing the watcher reads config.cue for. The datasource is one of the bundle's datasources, named like the others (redis, or redis-broker for the one tagged broker). Its password may be written inline or as a {file: …}; a {ref: …} is refused at startup, because the watcher has no secret manager.

Replicas that are not the leader stay idle. If the leader crashes, another replica acquires the lock within one TTL window (15 seconds for Redis).

The watcher keeps no state between polls: the orchestrator compares with its sync ledger. (watcher_state_datasource was removed; a config.cue that still sets it loads, with a log line.)

docs.title: Environment Resolution
docs.text:
When a webhook fires, varTrack resolves a single environment string from the event. This string is used to:

  • Resolve {env} in destination_template
  • Select the correct subtree from env-keyed config files
  • Determine which sink collection, prefix, or path to write to

docs.title: Resolution order
docs.text:
varTrack tries each strategy in order and uses the first one that produces a match:

Priority Strategy Example 1 branch_map[branch] main → production 2 file_path_map[file_path] configs/prod/** → production 3 pr_as_env: true PR #42 → pr-42 4 branch_as_env: true branch develop → develop 5 tag_as_env: true tag v1.2.3 → v1.2.3 6 fallback always → default

pr_as_env, branch_as_env and tag_as_env used to be called env_as_pr, env_as_branch and env_as_tags (and the S3 option prefix_as_env was env_as_prefix). The old names still work in config.cue, bundle.json and vartrack.json; varTrack logs a warning with the new name.

docs.title: branch_map — explicit mapping
docs.text:
Map specific branch names to environment names:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  branch_map: {
    main:    "production"
    develop: "staging"
    qa:      "qa"
  }
}]

Pushes to main write to production-config. Pushes to develop write to staging-config. Any branch not in the map falls through to the next strategy.

The web UI's Environments page lists every resolved environment with the branch it comes from and where it is written:

docs.title: file_path_map — path glob mapping
docs.text:
Map file paths (glob patterns) to environment names:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  file_path_map: {
    "configs/production/**": "production"
    "configs/staging/**":    "staging"
  }
}]

A push that changes configs/production/app.yaml resolves to production.

docs.title: pr_as_env — PR environments
docs.text:
pr_as_env: true

Pull request events resolve to pr-{number}. Useful for ephemeral preview environments.

PR #42  → env = "pr-42"
PR #103 → env = "pr-103"

docs.title: branch_as_env — branch name as environment
docs.text:
branch_as_env: true

The branch name becomes the environment name directly:

branch "develop"     → env = "develop"
branch "feature/foo" → env = "feature/foo"

docs.title: tag_as_env — tag name as environment
docs.text:
tag_as_env: true

Tag push events use the tag name as the environment:

tag "v1.2.3"    → env = "v1.2.3"
tag "release-5" → env = "release-5"

docs.title: root_key — extracting a subtree before slicing
docs.text:
If your config file has a wrapper key, set root_key in the rule to unwrap it first. varTrack extracts the subtree under that key, then runs env auto-detection on it.

rules: [{
  root_key: "vartrack"   // default — extract the "vartrack" subtree if it exists
}]

# configs/app.yaml
vartrack:
  production:
    database_host: mongo.prod.internal
  staging:
    database_host: mongo.staging.internal
other_tool:
  setting: ignored      # not under root_key — never touched

root_key: "vartrack" → extracts the inner dict → Pattern 1 runs on it → database_host=mongo.prod.internal for production.

Set root_key: "" to always process the whole file regardless of structure.

If the key doesn't exist in the file, varTrack soft-falls back to the whole file.

docs.title: Auto-detection from config file structure
docs.text: When your config file itself is keyed by environment, varTrack auto-detects the structure and extracts only the relevant slice — no extra rule config needed. Three patterns are supported.

docs.title: Pattern 1 — all top-level keys are env names
docs.text:
Every top-level value is a dict. varTrack merges default first, then the matching env overrides it.

# configs/app.yaml
production:
  database_host: mongo.prod.internal
  max_connections: 100
staging:
  database_host: mongo.staging.internal
  max_connections: 10
default:
  max_connections: 5    # fallback for unknown envs
  log_level: info
env result production database_host=mongo.prod.internal, max_connections=100, log_level=info staging database_host=mongo.staging.internal, max_connections=10, log_level=info pr-42 max_connections=5, log_level=info (from default)

docs.title: Pattern 2 — per-field env sub-keys mixed with scalars
docs.text:
Each field that varies per env has a dict of env→value. Fields that are the same across all envs are plain scalars.

# configs/app.yaml
database_host:
  production: mongo.prod.internal
  staging:    mongo.staging.internal
  default:    mongo.local
max_connections: 50     # same for every env — written as-is
log_level: info
env result production database_host=mongo.prod.internal, max_connections=50, log_level=info staging database_host=mongo.staging.internal, max_connections=50, log_level=info pr-42 database_host=mongo.local, max_connections=50, log_level=info

docs.title: Pattern 3 — env dicts and scalar defaults at the same level
docs.text:
Some keys at the same nesting level are env names (dicts with overrides), others are plain scalars that apply to every env. Order in the file doesn't matter — varTrack categorizes by value type, not position. The env dict is merged on top of the scalars.

{
    "production": { "name": "worn",  "db": "mongo.prod.internal" },
    "predev":     { "name": "dan",   "db": "mongo.dev.internal"  },
    "name":       "bob",
    "age":        33,
    "timeout":    30
}
env result production name=worn, db=mongo.prod.internal, age=33, timeout=30 predev name=dan, db=mongo.dev.internal, age=33, timeout=30 unknown (no match, no default dict) data returned unchanged

Add a default dict to handle unknown envs:

{
    "production": { "name": "worn" },
    "default":    { "name": "bob" },
    "age":        33
}

unknown env → name=bob, age=33.

docs.title: Pattern 3 — env-named top-level dicts mixed with scalar defaults
docs.text:
{
    "prod":   { "name": "worn" },
    "predev": { "name": "dan" },
    "name":   "bob",
    "age":    33
}

Top-level dicts whose key matches the resolved env are applied as overrides. Top-level scalars are universal defaults merged underneath:

env result prod name=worn, age=33 predev name=dan, age=33 unknown (no matching dict, no default dict) data returned unchanged

You can also include a default dict for unknown env fallback:

{
    "prod":    { "name": "worn" },
    "default": { "name": "bob" },
    "age":     33
}

unknown env → name=bob, age=33.

docs.title: default fallback
docs.text: In all three patterns, if the resolved env has no matching key, varTrack silently falls back to default. If there is no default either, the data is returned unchanged.

docs.title: root_key — extracting a subtree before slicing
docs.text:
Real config files often live alongside other tooling config (Spring, Maven, npm, etc.). Use root_key to extract only the varTrack-relevant subtree before env-detection runs.

rules: [{
  root_key: "vartrack"   // default — extract "vartrack" subtree if present
}]

Set root_key: "" to always process the whole file. If the key doesn't exist, varTrack soft-falls back to the whole file.

docs.title: Example — package.json
docs.text:
A Node.js project that also carries deploy config inside package.json:

{
  "name": "my-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "scripts": { "start": "node index.js" },
  "vartrack": {
    "production": { "API_URL": "https://api.prod.com",  "LOG_LEVEL": "warn"  },
    "staging":    { "API_URL": "https://api.stg.com",   "LOG_LEVEL": "info"  },
    "default":    { "API_URL": "https://api.local.com", "LOG_LEVEL": "debug" }
  }
}

rules: [{
  file_name: "package.json"
  root_key:  "vartrack"       // ignore name/version/scripts — only sync vartrack block
  branch_map: { main: "production", develop: "staging" }
}]

Push to main → API_URL=https://api.prod.com, LOG_LEVEL=warn written to the sink.

docs.title: Example — pom.xml (Maven)
docs.text:
A Java project with deploy properties in pom.xml. varTrack parses XML and extracts the subtree:

<project>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-service</artifactId>

  <vartrack>
    <production>
      <database_host>mongo.prod.internal</database_host>
      <max_connections>100</max_connections>
    </production>
    <staging>
      <database_host>mongo.staging.internal</database_host>
      <max_connections>10</max_connections>
    </staging>
    <default>
      <max_connections>5</max_connections>
    </default>
  </vartrack>
</project>

rules: [{
  file_name: "pom.xml"
  root_key:  "vartrack"
  branch_map: { main: "production", develop: "staging" }
}]

Push to main → database_host=mongo.prod.internal, max_connections=100.

docs.title: Combining strategies
docs.text:
Strategies can be combined. varTrack uses the first one that matches:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  branch_map: {
    main:    "production"   // explicit — highest priority
    develop: "staging"
  }
  pr_as_env:     true       // fallback for PRs not in branch_map
  branch_as_env: true       // fallback for all other branches
}]
Event Resolved env Push to main production (from branch_map) Push to develop staging (from branch_map) PR #42 opened pr-42 (from pr_as_env) Push to feature/x feature/x (from branch_as_env)

docs.title: Sync Strategies
docs.text: A sync strategy controls how varTrack applies the flattened config values to a datasource. The right strategy depends on the size of your config and how often you need reads vs. writes.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
AUTO (recommended)GIT_UPSERT_ALLGIT_SMART_REPAIRLIVE_STATE

varTrack picks the strategy automatically based on payload size:

  • ≤ 500 keys → GIT_UPSERT_ALL

  • 500 keys → GIT_SMART_REPAIR

This is the default and works well for most configurations. No tuning needed.

sync_mode: "AUTO"

Writes every key from the flattened Git payload to the datasource in one bulk operation. Does not read the current state first.

Best for: Small configs (< 500 keys), initial bootstrapping, or when you always want a clean overwrite.

sync_mode: "SYNC_MODE_GIT_UPSERT_ALL"
Read before write No Keys written All Stale key cleanup Only if prune: true set Best for Small configs

Reads the current live state first, computes a diff (added / changed / removed keys), and writes only the differences. Uses BLAKE3 content hashing to detect unchanged values.

Best for: Large configs (> 500 keys), or datasources where minimizing write operations matters.

sync_mode: "SYNC_MODE_GIT_SMART_REPAIR"
Read before write Yes Keys written Changed only Stale key cleanup Yes, on diff Best for Large configs

Replaces the entire stored state with Git's current view. No diff computed — direct overwrite.

Best for: Low-latency sinks, or scenarios where the simplest possible write path matters more than efficiency.

sync_mode: "SYNC_MODE_LIVE_STATE"

docs.title: Setting the strategy
docs.text:
Override per rule in config.cue:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  sync_mode:  "SYNC_MODE_GIT_SMART_REPAIR"
}]

Or let AUTO decide — just omit sync_mode or set it to "AUTO".

Each mode can be written short ("AUTO", "GIT_SMART_REPAIR") or as its full proto name ("SYNC_MODE_AUTO", "SYNC_MODE_GIT_SMART_REPAIR"); both load.

docs.title: Stale key pruning
docs.text:
When keys are removed from your Git config file, varTrack can delete them from the datasource:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  sync_mode:  "AUTO"
  prune:      true     // delete keys present in datasource but missing from Git
}]

Warning

prune: true permanently deletes keys from the datasource that are no longer in Git. Use prune: {enabled: true, dry_run: true} or the full dry-run first to verify what would be removed.

docs.title: What prune deletes
docs.text:
Prune runs once per environment, after all of its files are written, and only if none of them failed. So a key that moved from one file to another is never deleted, and there is nothing to configure for multi-file rules.

A key is stale when varTrack wrote it before and no file of the environment holds it any more. Prune deletes nothing else:

  • A key somebody else put in the datasource is never deleted, with or without protection.
  • A stale key that was changed outside varTrack since varTrack wrote it is kept, and reported with a PruneSkipped event.
  • Environments that write to the same place keep each other's keys: Vercel's staging and develop both write to preview, and a Redis key_prefix or a ZooKeeper path without {env} is shared by every environment.
  • So do datasources and tenants. A datasource's name says nothing about where it writes. Two datasources on the same Redis database (same servers and db) with the same key_prefix and hash, the same ZooKeeper servers and root path, or the same Vercel team, project and targets write the same keys, and one never prunes a key the other still holds. A datasource on another server, or with another prefix, is not compared. MongoDB filters its documents by tenant, datasource and environment, so its datasources never share keys. Who holds a key is recorded with each sync, as the key space the sync wrote to, so another tenant counts even when its schema repository cannot be read right now. A target last written by an older version has no such record and is placed by the rules until it is written again. When a prune finds another target holding keys in the same key space, the UI shows one Shared key space warning event for the environment (again after the sharing has ended and begun anew).
  • If the rules of the tenants cannot be listed when prune runs, nothing is pruned, as when the ledger cannot be read.
  • If the delete fails, the sync still succeeds. The keys stay on the list and the next sync retries them (a PruneFailed event).

Prune applies to sinks that keep each key separately: Redis (hash or strings), Vercel, ZooKeeper and MongoDB with update_strategy: "STRATEGY_KEY_VALUE". A sink that replaces a whole object on every write — ConfigMap, S3, Linux server, Helm, MongoDB with its default STRATEGY_DOCUMENT (or STRATEGY_FILE), Redis with the JSON structure — has no stale key to delete. Setting prune on one has no effect.

prune.last was removed: the delete is always last now. A prune block that only had last is a disabled block; write prune: true or prune: {enabled: true}.

docs.title: prune.protection
docs.text:
Glob patterns for keys that must never be deleted, even if they're absent from Git. A pattern is matched against the flat key, like db.host, before the sink formats it for its own layout:

rules: [{
  prune: {
    enabled:    true
    protection: ["SYSTEM_*", "_vt_*", "readonly.*"]
  }
}]

prune_protection, the former flat name, is still read from bundle.json and vartrack.json; config.cue only takes the prune block.

docs.title: Full dry-run — simulate the entire sync
docs.text:
No writes, no deletes. Returns a full report of what would be written, changed, and deleted. The keys prune would see as stale are listed per environment under prune.would_delete; whether something changed one outside varTrack is only known when a real sync reads it.

# Via CLI
vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env staging --dry-run

# Via HTTP
POST /v1/webhooks/mongo/dry-run

@secret-annotated fields are fetched from Vault but masked as *** in the report.

In the web UI, Dry run on a rule runs the same simulation for the environments you pick:

docs.title: Prune dry-run — simulate deletes only
docs.text:
Test the prune step independently without touching any writes. Enabled per rule:

rules: [{
  prune: {
    enabled: true
    dry_run: true   // always simulate deletes — never actually remove keys
  }
}]

With prune.dry_run, every sync runs normally (writes go through) but the delete step is always simulated, never executed. The task reports the stale keys, and they stay on the list: turn dry_run off and the next sync deletes them.

docs.title: CUE Schema Annotations
docs.text: varTrack supports two custom annotations in CUE schema files: @secret() and @logger(). Both are declared on fields in your schema, not in your config files.

docs.title: @secret()
docs.text: Marks a field whose value is a Vault path at ETL time instead of a real value. Before writing to any sink, the orchestrator reads the schema, finds every @secret-annotated field, fetches the real value from Vault, and injects it in-place.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
// default secret manager
"db.password": string @secret()

// named secret manager (matches secret_managers[].vault tag in the bundle)
"api_key": string @secret(ref="other-vault")

docs.title: Config file side
docs.text:
In the actual config file being synced (YAML, JSON, TOML, etc.) the field value is the Vault path:

# configs/app.yaml
database:
  password: "@secret(secret/myapp/db#password)"

auth:
  jwt_secret: "@secret(secret/myapp/auth#jwt_secret)"

The format is @secret(mount/path#field) — mount path + # + field name inside the Vault secret.

docs.title: What happens at ETL time
docs.text:
1. Parse schema → find @secret-annotated fields
2. For each field present in flat_data:
   a. Determine secret manager: ref= or "default"
   b. Fetch value from Vault: the path and field from "@secret(mount/path#field)"
      (the manager's mount point may lead the path)
   c. Replace flat_data[field] with the real value
3. Write to sink — Vault value arrives, not the path string

docs.title: Dry-run behaviour
docs.text: In dry-run mode, @secret fields are masked as *** in the report. The real value is fetched from Vault but never returned to the caller.

docs.title: Bundle wiring
docs.text:
The ref= value must match the tag of a secret manager declared in the bundle:

bundle: {
  secret_managers: [
    {
      vault: {
        tag:         "default"   // matched by @secret()
        endpoint:    "https://vault.mycompany.com"
        mount_point: "secret"
        kv_version:  2
        token_auth: { token: "hvs.xxxx" }
      }
    },
    {
      vault: {
        tag:         "other-vault"   // matched by @secret(ref="other-vault")
        endpoint:    "https://vault2.mycompany.com"
        mount_point: "secret"
        kv_version:  2
        token_auth: { token: "hvs.yyyy" }
      }
    },
  ]
}

@secret() without ref= uses the rule's secret_manager when it names one, else the entry tagged default, else the bundle's only one. Secret managers are declared in config.cue's secret_managers only; a rule's own secrets block was removed. A field whose value is not in the @secret(path#field) form is read at the manager's path_prefix, under the field's own name.

docs.title: @logger()
docs.text: Marks a field for structured change logging. Every time a value changes between ETL runs, the orchestrator emits an INFO log entry showing the field name, old value, new value, datasource, and environment.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
app_port:      int    @logger()
database.host: string @logger()

docs.title: Log output
docs.text:
When a non-secret field changes:

field changed  datasource=mongo  env=production  field=app_port
               from=8080  to=9090  file=configs/app.yaml

When a field is written for the first time (no old value):

field changed  datasource=mongo  env=production  field=database.host
               to="db.prod.internal"  file=configs/app.yaml

docs.title: Combining with @secret()
docs.text:
You can annotate a field with both. The change is logged but the values are never revealed — only changed=true is recorded:

"database.password": string @secret() @logger()

field changed  datasource=mongo  env=production  field=database.password
               changed=true  file=configs/app.yaml

docs.title: Full schema example
docs.text:
// schemas/myapp.cue
#Config: {
  app_port:          int & >=1024 & <=65535   @logger()
  log_level:         "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error"
  "database.host":   string & !=""            @logger()
  "database.port":   int                      @logger()
  "database.password": string & !=""          @secret() @logger()
  "api.secret_key":  string & !=""            @secret()
  max_connections:   int & >=1 & <=1000
}

Register the schema in your bundle:

bundle: {
  schema_registry: {
    platform: "github"
    repo:     "my-org/schemas"
    branch:   "main"
  }
  // ...
}

varTrack fetches the schema from Git, runs cue vet to validate the payload, then processes @secret and @logger annotations before writing to any sink.

docs.title: Authentication & Authorization
docs.text: varTrack's CLI API (/v1/cli/*, used by vt) keeps no users or roles of its own. The caller shows their own Git token, and the rule's Git platform says what they may do. An optional OPA policy then decides with the whole request.

docs.title: Git permissions
docs.text:
vt sends the caller's Git token for the rule's platform — a GitHub or Gitea personal access token — as Authorization: Bearer <token>:

vt login --server https://gateway.example.com --token <your Git token>

For each request the gateway asks the platform of the rule that syncs to the datasource who the token belongs to (GET /user) and what they may do in the rule's repositories (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}, and GET /user/repos for patterns such as acme/*):

The caller can, in one of the rule's repositories… …so they may push vt sync read vt sync --dry-run, vt validate, vt task

A rule's repositories are the ones its repositories and enabled overrides name or match, minus its exclusions — the repositories the gateway routes pushes from. The web UI decides the same way (see below).

Answer When 401 no token, or the platform rejects it 403 the caller lacks the access above, or the OPA policy denies the request 404 no rule syncs to the datasource; a task of a rule the caller cannot read

vt validate without --datasource, and vt validate-config, need a token any platform of the bundle accepts. vt task list shows the tasks of the rules the caller can read.

The platform:login entries of ui.auth.admins may do anything, on the CLI API as in the UI. Tasks record their caller as login@platform.

The bundle's auth.oidc and auth.rbac blocks are no longer used; the gateway logs a warning when they are set.

docs.title: OPA — policy layer (Open Policy Agent)
docs.text:
OPA runs after the Git permission check for decisions Git permissions can't express — e.g., "writers may sync anywhere but production". Give the policy in exactly one of three ways:

auth: {
  opa: {
    inline_policy: """
      package vartrack.authz

      default allow = false

      # validate and task reads: Git read access has decided
      allow {
        input.action != "sync"
      }

      # anyone who may push syncs outside production
      allow {
        input.action == "sync"
        input.env    != "production"
      }

      # only repository admins sync production
      allow {
        input.action == "sync"
        input.env    == "production"
        input.user.permission == "admin"
      }
    """

    // policy_file: "/etc/vartrack/policy.rego"                      // a file on the gateway
    // server_url:  "http://opa:8181/v1/data/vartrack/authz/allow"  // a remote OPA server
  }
}

The policy must be in package vartrack.authz and define allow; anything but allow == true denies the request. Policies are written in Rego v0 syntax (allow { … }), as above. To write Rego v1 syntax (allow if { … }, x in xs), start the policy with import rego.v1.

inline_policy and policy_file are compiled in-process (tens of microseconds per decision) — no OPA server required. With server_url the gateway asks that server instead: point it at the rule (…/v1/data/vartrack/authz/allow) or at the package (…/v1/data/vartrack/authz, whose allow is then read). A server that cannot be reached, answers anything but 2xx, or takes longer than five seconds denies the request with 500. A policy that does not compile, or a policy file that cannot be read, stops the gateway at startup.

A full example policy — admins sync anywhere, writers outside production but never configs/secrets/*, dry runs anywhere — is at examples/policies/vartrack_authz.rego.

docs.title: OPA input document
docs.text:
Every request evaluation receives:

Field Example input.user.login "alice" — on the rule's platform input.user.platform "gitea" input.user.permission "admin", "write" or "read" — in the rule's repositories input.user.admin true for ui.auth.admins entries input.user.repositories ["acme/configs"] — the rule's repository names and patterns input.action "sync", "validate" input.resource "datasource" input.datasource "mongo" input.env "production" (lower-cased) input.file_path "configs/app.yaml" input.tenant_id "acme" input.dry_run false

docs.title: Reloading the policy
docs.text: POST /admin/opa/reload on the gateway's admin port (ADMIN_ADDR, default :9090) recompiles the policy and re-reads policy_file. If the new policy does not compile, the call answers 422 with the compile error and the previous policy stays in force. A policy_file is also re-read every OPA_RELOAD_INTERVAL (default 30m).

docs.title: Layer evaluation order
docs.text:
Request
  │
  ▼
Git token             ← 401 if missing, or the rule's platform rejects it
  │
  ▼
Git permission        ← 403 without push (sync) or read (anything else) access
  │
  ▼
OPA evaluation        ← 403 if the policy does not allow it
  │
  ▼
Handler

OPA is skipped if no opa block is configured.

docs.title: Web UI sign-in with your Git platform
docs.text:
The web UI can sign users in with the Git platforms your rules already use (GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, Gitea) and show each user only what those platforms let them see. varTrack keeps no list of who may see what: each rule is judged on its own platform, asked with the user's own account there.

The user can, on the rule's platform… …so in the UI they read at least one repository the rule covers see the rule, its tasks and its events read the repository an environment was last synced from see that environment, its keys and its diff write to one of the rule's repositories can Sync it; with read access only they can Dry run it

A rule covers the repositories it names, the ones its patterns (acme/*) match minus its exclusions, and the ones its environments were synced from. A rule, environment or task the user cannot see answers not found, exactly like one that does not exist. Answers are cached for two minutes per session, so a permission change on a platform shows up within that time.

docs.title: Tenants are shown, not chosen
docs.text:
The UI covers every tenant at once: a rule, task or event carries its tenant, and what a person sees is what Git lets them read, whichever tenant it belongs to. There is no tenant to switch to.

Who Sees Sign-in is off every rule of every tenant An admin (ui.auth.admins) every rule of every tenant A signed-in user every rule, of any tenant, whose repository their account can read on the rule's platform. A tenant with no such rule does not appear at all.

When the viewer sees more than one tenant, the Rules, Environments, Events and Tasks pages show the tenant and offer a Tenant filter that lists only those tenants. The same platform/datasource can exist in two tenants, so a rule is identified by its tenant too: /rules/{tenant}/{platform}/{datasource}; a link without the tenant still opens the rule when only one visible tenant has it.

A rule you cannot see because you have not connected its platform is counted, never named: the Rules page says "3 rules on gitea are hidden" with a Connect gitea button. Rules on a platform you are connected to, in repositories your account cannot read, are not counted — that would show that a private repository's rules exist.

The UI API takes an optional ?tenant= (or the X-Tenant-ID header) to narrow an answer to one tenant. It narrows only: it never shows a rule the viewer cannot read.

docs.title: Rules on several platforms
docs.text: With rules on GitHub and on Gitea, add a provider for each. Users sign in with either one and connect the other from the sign-in page, the user menu or their profile — the same session then holds both accounts, and each rule is judged with the account on its own platform. A GitHub rule is never judged by a Gitea account, even when the repository names match. Until a platform is connected, its rules stay hidden and the UI says how many there are. Signing out ends the session on every platform. Rules on a platform without sign-in set up are hidden from everyone but admins.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Register an OAuth application on each platform, all with the same callback URL: {public_url}/api/orchestrator/v1/auth/callback — for example http://localhost:8080/api/orchestrator/v1/auth/callback.
    • GitHub: Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps. GitHub OAuth Apps can only read private repositories with the repo scope, which is the default here.
    • Gitea: Settings → Applications → OAuth2 Applications, confidential client. Default scopes: read:user read:repository.
  2. Add a ui block to the bundle (config.cue), with one provider per platform users sign in with:
bundle: {
  platforms: [
    {github: {endpoint: "https://github.com", ...}},
    {gitea:  {endpoint: "http://gitea:3000", ...}},
  ]

  ui: {
    public_url: "https://vartrack.example.com"   // where users open the UI
    auth: {
      providers: [
        {
          platform:      "github"                // a platform's name from platforms
          client_id:     "Iv1.8a61f9b3a7aba766"
          client_secret: {file: "/run/secrets/github-oauth"}
        },
        {
          platform:      "gitea"
          client_id:     {file: "/run/secrets/gitea-oauth-id"}
          client_secret: {ref: {path: "ui/gitea", key: "client_secret"}}   // from Vault
          browser_url:   "https://gitea.example.com"   // when the platform's endpoint is internal
        },
      ]
      admins: ["github:octo-admin"]              // optional: see and sync every rule
      secret_manager: "vault"                    // optional with a single secret manager
    }
  }
}
Field Default Description ui.public_url http://localhost:5173 Where users open the UI; the callback is built from it ui.auth.providers[].platform — A platform's name from platforms: github, gitea, gitea-team… ui.auth.providers[].client_id / client_secret — The OAuth application: a string, {value: "…"}, {file: "/path"} or {ref: {path: "…", key: "…"}} ui.auth.providers[].browser_url the platform's endpoint The platform's address as the browser sees it, when the endpoint is internal (e.g. http://gitea:3000) ui.auth.providers[].scopes per platform, see above OAuth scopes ui.auth.admins — platform:login entries that see every rule; with one provider a bare login works. With several, an admin must name the platform: alice on GitHub and alice on Gitea need not be the same person ui.auth.session_ttl_seconds 28800 How long a session lasts (8 hours) ui.auth.session_secret derived from the client secrets Key for encrypting sessions at rest ui.auth.redirect_url {public_url}/api/orchestrator/v1/auth/callback The callback URL, when it differs ui.auth.secret_manager the bundle's only secret manager Which entry of secret_managers {ref: …} values come from, by name: vault, or vault-{tag} for a tagged one. Needed when there are several

Without ui.auth the UI is open to anyone who can reach it, as before. If sign-in is set up but cannot work — a missing secret, a file that can't be read, an unknown platform — the UI stays closed and says it is misconfigured; the orchestrator's log says why.

{ref: {path, key}} reads field key of the Vault secret at path (under the secret manager's mount_point). The orchestrator reads files and references when it loads these settings, then again at most once a minute, so a rotated secret is picked up without a restart. If Vault can't be reached or the key is missing, the UI stays closed and the orchestrator's log names the field. Rotating a client secret also ends the sessions in progress unless session_secret is set, since the session key is otherwise derived from the client secrets. The model is ui.proto.

Without a ui.auth block, the orchestrator reads the same settings from environment variables: UI_AUTH_PLATFORMS (github,gitea), then per platform UI_AUTH_{P}_CLIENT_ID, UI_AUTH_{P}_CLIENT_SECRET, UI_AUTH_{P}_URL and UI_AUTH_{P}_SCOPES ({P} is the platform name upper-cased with - as _), plus UI_PUBLIC_URL, UI_AUTH_REDIRECT_URL, UI_AUTH_ADMINS, UI_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS and UI_SESSION_SECRET. Any of them can be read from a file by appending _FILE.

docs.title: How sessions work
docs.text:
Sign-in is the OAuth2 authorization code flow with PKCE. The login state is single-use, expires after five minutes, names the platform, and is bound to the browser that started it by a cookie. After sign-in the browser holds only a random session id in an HttpOnly cookie (Secure when the UI is served over HTTPS). The platform tokens stay on the server, encrypted with AES-256-GCM, in Redis next to the sync ledger, and expired tokens are refreshed when the platform issues refresh tokens. Signing out deletes the session on the server, so a copied cookie stops working too.

This covers the web UI's API (/v1/ui/*). The CLI API (/v1/cli/*, used by vt and by the UI's Playground) takes a Git token instead, as above; paste one under API token for the Playground on the sign-in page to use it from the UI.

docs.title: Bundle Reference
docs.text: All three varTrack services read a single shared CUE bundle (config.cue). The bundle declares your platforms, datasources, routing rules, schema registry, and secret managers.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
bundle: {
  platforms: [{
    github: {
      endpoint:        "https://github.com"
      push_event_name: "push"
      pr_event_name:   "pull_request"
      secret:          "my-webhook-secret"
    }
  }]

  datasources: [{
    mongo: {
      endpoint:   "mongodb://localhost:27017"
      database:   "vartrack"
      collection: "variables"
    }
  }]

  rules: [{
    platform:             "github"
    datasource:           "mongo"
    file_name:            "configs/app.yaml"
    repositories:         ["my-org/*"]
    destination_template: "{env}-config"
    self_heal:            true
    branch_map: {
      main:    "production"
      develop: "staging"
    }
  }]
}

docs.title: platforms
docs.text: Declares which Git platforms send webhooks to varTrack.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
platforms: [{
  github: {
    endpoint:        "https://github.com"     // or your GHE URL
    protocol:        "https"                  // "https" or "ssh"
    push_event_name: "push"
    pr_event_name:   "pull_request"
    secret:          "my-secret"              // webhook HMAC secret
    token:           "ghp_xxx"               // PAT for cloning + repo listing
    org_name:        "my-org"                 // optional — scope to one org
    verify_ssl:      true
    timeout:         "30s"
  }
}]

Multiple platform instances can be declared with different tag values:

platforms: [
  { github: { tag: "public",     endpoint: "https://github.com", ... } },
  { github: { tag: "enterprise", endpoint: "https://git.mycompany.com", ... } },
]

docs.title: datasources
docs.text: Declares where config values should be written. Every datasource has an optional tag to distinguish multiple instances of the same type.

docs.title: MongoDB
docs.text:
datasources: [{
  mongo: {
    tag:             ""                        // optional — "mongo-{tag}" if set
    endpoint:        "mongodb://mongo:27017"
    database:        "vartrack"
    collection:      "variables"
    update_strategy: "STRATEGY_DOCUMENT"       // the default; or "STRATEGY_KEY_VALUE", "STRATEGY_FILE": see the MongoDB sink
  }
}]

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
datasources: [{
  redis: {
    host:     "redis"
    port:     6379
    password: "secret"
    db:       0
  }
}]

docs.title: ZooKeeper
docs.text:
datasources: [{
  zookeeper: {
    hosts:    ["zookeeper:2181"]
    base_path: "/vartrack"
  }
}]

docs.title: S3
docs.text:
datasources: [{
  s3: {
    bucket:           "my-config-bucket"
    region:           "us-east-1"
    access_key_id:     "AKIA..."
    secret_access_key: "..."
  }
}]

For all datasource options see the individual sink pages.

docs.title: rules
docs.text:
Rules map a platform + file combination to a datasource and define how data is written. They are the first of the layers a rule is built from: a tenant's bundle.json and a repository's vartrack.json can change some of their settings, and force pins the ones they may not.

A rule is identified by its platform and datasource. Each pair has at most one rule, and varTrack refuses to start when two share it; to write a second destination in the same database, declare a tagged datasource for it and give it its own rule. Rules on different platforms may write to the same datasource: a webhook is then told apart by the event header of the platform that sent it (X-Gitea-Event, X-GitHub-Event), and vt sync and vt validate need --platform to say which rule they mean.

Two platforms of the same type (say two GitHub hosts) send the same headers, so the webhook secret tells them apart: the gateway checks the signature of the delivery against each candidate platform's secret and uses the one that signed it. Give each of them its own secret. A delivery signed by none of them is refused (401); when two share a secret, or none has one, or signatures are not checked (a non-production gateway), the webhook is refused as ambiguous (400).

rules: [{
  platform:             "github"              // matches platform name (or "github-{tag}")
  datasource:           "mongo"               // matches datasource name (or "mongo-{tag}")
  file_name:            "configs/app.yaml"    // file path in the repo to watch
  repositories:         ["my-org/*"]          // glob patterns — which repos trigger this

  // Where data lands
  destination_template: "{env}-config"

  // Source (pick one)
  file_name:     "configs/app.yaml"           // single file tracked in all repos
  // file_path_map: { production: "configs/prod.yaml", staging: "configs/staging.yaml" }

  // Repository filtering
  exclude_repositories: ["my-org/legacy-.*"] // negative glob patterns
  // overrides: [{match_repositories: ["other-org/*"], enable: true}]

  // Root key extraction (optional)
  root_key: "vartrack"                        // extract subtree before flattening
                                              // set to "" to process the whole file

  // Variable overlay (optional)
  variables_map: {
    REGION: "us-east-1"                       // inject or override any key
  }

  // Environment resolution
  branch_map: {
    main:    "production"
    develop: "staging"
  }
  pr_as_env:     false
  branch_as_env: false
  tag_as_env:    false

  // Sync behavior
  sync_mode:     "AUTO"                       // AUTO, GIT_UPSERT_ALL, GIT_SMART_REPAIR, LIVE_STATE
                                              // (SYNC_MODE_AUTO etc. work too)
  prune: {
    enabled:    false                         // delete keys no longer in Git
    protection: ["SYSTEM_*", "_vt_*"]         // glob patterns for keys that must never be deleted
  }

  // Validation
  strict_validation: false                    // true: a file the CUE schema rejects fails the sync
                                              // (default: the failure is logged and the file is synced)

  // Drift detection
  self_heal:     true                         // auto-repair on drift
  drift_ignore:  ["feature_flags.*"]          // keys the application changes itself: shown, never drift

  // Pausing
  suspend:       false                        // true: pushes and self-heal skip the rule

  // Keys no tenant bundle.json or repo vartrack.json can change: applied last
  force: {prune: {enabled: false}}
}]

repositories, exclude_repositories, overrides, self_heal and secret_manager are set here only, as are the datasources' connection settings: a tenant's bundle.json cannot change them. force holds the other keys this rule pins.

suspend pauses the rule without removing it, for an incident or a migration. A push and the watcher's self-heal skip a suspended rule, and the drift check does not compare it. A sync started by hand, from the web UI or vt, still runs, so an incident or a migration does not block a deliberate sync. The web UI shows the rule as suspended.

drift_ignore lists glob patterns of keys the application changes itself, such as a feature-flag counter or a rotated token. The drift check still shows them, as ignored, but never counts them as drift and the watcher does not heal them; a sync still writes them.

strict_validation decides what a failed CUE schema check does. Off (the default), the failure is logged as a warning and the file is synced; on, the file is not written and the sync fails. A repository can turn it on in its vartrack.json.

docs.title: Per-repo overrides
docs.text:
Individual repositories can override a subset of their rule settings without touching config.cue. Add a vartrack.json file at the root of the repository:

{
  "root_key": "app_config",
  "branch_map": { "main": "production", "staging": "staging" },
  "prune": true
}

Keys in vartrack.json are merged on top of the rule for that repository on every webhook (branch_map, file_path_map, variables_map and prune key by key), and the rule's force keys are applied after them. Infrastructure keys (platform, datasource, token, repositories, self_heal, …) are always taken from the bundle and cannot be overridden. The schema registry is unaffected.

See the full Per-Repo Overrides reference for the complete list of overridable keys, security model, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: schema_registry
docs.text:
Points varTrack to a Git repo containing CUE schemas for validation:

schema_registry: {
  platform: "github"
  repo:     "my-org/schemas"
  branch:   "main"
}

When a webhook arrives, varTrack validates the parsed config against the tenant's CUE schema before writing anything. Invalid payloads are rejected with a descriptive error.

The schema repo can also hold bundle.json (or rules.json): the tenant's rule settings, laid over the rules here. It only holds what the tenant adds or changes — nothing has to be repeated or kept in sync. See the Schema Registry reference for how a rule is built from the layers, the full repo structure, the bundle.json format, tenant env vars, and caching behaviour.

docs.title: secret_managers
docs.text:
Secrets referenced in the bundle (tokens, passwords) can be resolved from HashiCorp Vault:

secret_managers: [{
  vault: {
    endpoint:    "https://vault.mycompany.com"
    mount_point: "secret"
    kv_version:  2
    path_prefix: "myapp/prod"   // optional: where a plain @secret() field is read (see below)

    // Auth — pick one:
    token_auth: {
      token: "hvs.xxxx"
    }
    // app_role_auth: {
    //   role_id:   "role-id"
    //   secret_id: "secret-id"
    // }
    // kubernetes_auth: {
    //   role:            "vartrack"
    //   jwt_path:        "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
    // }
    // userpass_auth: {
    //   username: "vartrack"
    //   password: "pass"
    // }
  }
}]

path_prefix is for the CUE schema's @secret() fields. A field whose value in the config file is written as @secret(mount/path#key) names its own secret and does not use it. A field left as a plain value is read from the secret at path_prefix, under the field's own name, so database.password is the key database.password of the secret secret/myapp/prod.

A rule used to carry its own Vault settings in a secrets block. That block was removed: declare the manager here, and name it in the rule's secret_manager when there is more than one. A config that still sets secrets loads, with a warning that says so.

docs.title: Secret value forms
docs.text:
Credential fields in the bundle — a platform's token and secret, a datasource's password, private_key, access_key_id, secret_access_key, the web UI's client_id and client_secret — accept three forms:

// 1. Plain string — value written directly in the bundle
token: "ghp_xxx"

// 2. File reference — read from a file on the service's machine
//    Ideal for Docker secrets, Kubernetes secret mounts, or any on-disk secret
token:    {file: "/run/secrets/github-token"}                  // the whole file, whitespace stripped
password: {file: "/run/secrets/db.env", key: "DB_PASSWORD"}    // one key of the file

// 3. Vault reference — fetched from HashiCorp Vault at ETL time
//    Requires a secret_managers block in the bundle
token: {ref: {path: "vartrack/github", key: "token"}}

Two credentials take only a plain string: a MongoDB datasource's password, and a Vault secret manager's own credentials (token_auth.token, app_role_auth.secret_id, …).

A {ref: …} is read from an entry of secret_managers. A rule's secret_manager names the entry for everything that rule uses — its platform's credentials and its datasource's — and for its @secret() fields:

rules: [{
  platform:       "github"
  datasource:     "redis"
  secret_manager: "vault-prod"    // a secret_managers entry: "vault", or "vault-{tag}"
}]

A rule without one uses the entry tagged default, else the bundle's only one.

With key, a {file: …} is parsed by its extension — .json, .yaml/.yml, otherwise KEY=value lines (.env, .properties) — and the key's value is the credential; in JSON and YAML a dotted key (db.password) reaches into nested objects. Without key the whole file is the credential. An SSH private_key is the exception: it must be a key file of its own.

{file: …} is read on the machine of the service that uses the credential: the gateway for platform credentials, the orchestrator for datasource credentials. A credential both use — a platform token — needs its file on both.

docs.title: {file:} — mounted secret files
docs.text:
The {file:} form keeps secrets completely out of the bundle. Mount the file via Docker or Kubernetes and point to it:

secret_managers: [{
  vault: {
    endpoint:    "https://vault.mycompany.com"
    mount_point: "secret"
    kv_version:  2
    token_auth: {
      token: {file: "/run/secrets/vault-token"}   // Docker secret or K8s secret volume
    }
  }
}]

platforms: [{
  github: {
    endpoint: "https://github.com"
    token:    {file: "/run/secrets/github-pat"}
    secret:   {file: "/run/secrets/github-webhook-secret"}
  }
}]

Docker Compose example:

services:
  gateway:
    image: vartrack/gateway
    secrets:
      - github-pat
      - github-webhook-secret

secrets:
  github-pat:
    file: ./secrets/github-pat.txt
  github-webhook-secret:
    file: ./secrets/github-webhook-secret.txt

Kubernetes example:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: vartrack-secrets
stringData:
  github-pat: ghp_xxx
  github-webhook-secret: my-secret
---
# In the Pod spec:
volumeMounts:
  - name: vartrack-secrets
    mountPath: /run/secrets
    readOnly: true
volumes:
  - name: vartrack-secrets
    secret:
      secretName: vartrack-secrets

If the file cannot be read at startup, the service exits with a descriptive error.

docs.title: global_tags
docs.text:
Arbitrary key-value metadata applied to every write across all sinks:

global_tags: {
  team:        "platform"
  environment: "production"
}

docs.title: Infrastructure wiring
docs.text:
Wire varTrack's internal components to specific datasources. Each value is the datasource name ({type} or {type}-{tag}):

bundle: {
  celery_broker_datasource:            "redis"        // Celery task queue broker
  celery_backend_datasource:           "redis"        // Celery result backend
  gateway_nonce_datasource:            "redis"        // replay-protection nonce store
  watcher_leader_election_datasource:  "redis"        // distributed leader election (Redis or ZooKeeper)
}

In a single-Redis setup, all four can point to the same datasource. In production you may want separate instances for isolation. The watcher_leader_election_datasource also accepts "zookeeper".

See Drift Detection for how the watcher uses these.

docs.title: ui
docs.text:
The web UI: where users open it, and sign-in with your Git platforms. Each user sees the rules whose repositories their own account on the rule's platform can read, and syncs the ones it can write to. Without ui.auth the UI is open.

ui: {
  public_url: "https://vartrack.example.com"
  auth: {
    providers: [
      {platform: "github", client_id: "Iv1.8a61…", client_secret: {file: "/run/secrets/github-oauth"}},
      {platform: "gitea",  client_id: {file: "/run/secrets/gitea-id"}, client_secret: {ref: {path: "ui/gitea", key: "client_secret"}},
       browser_url: "https://gitea.example.com"},
    ]
    admins: ["github:octo-admin"]
    secret_manager: "vault"   // where {ref: …} values come from; optional with one secret manager
  }
}

Every field, and how sessions work: Web UI sign-in. Full example: 15_web_ui_sign_in.cue.

docs.title: auth
docs.text:
The CLI API (/v1/cli/*, used by vt and the web UI's Playground) lets a caller do what their own Git token may do in the rule's repositories. auth adds an optional OPA policy on top:

auth: {
  opa: {policy_file: "/etc/vartrack/vartrack_authz.rego"}
}

How callers are checked, the OPA input document and the evaluation order: Authentication & Authorization. Full example: 13_cli_auth_opa.cue.

docs.title: Gateway tuning
docs.text: Fine-tune gateway-service behaviour directly from the bundle:

docs.title: max_webhook_body_bytes
docs.text:
Maximum size of an incoming webhook request body. Requests larger than this limit are rejected with HTTP 413. Defaults to 10 MiB when unset.

bundle: {
  max_webhook_body_bytes: 5242880   // 5 MiB
}
Value Effect 0 or unset Use the default (10 MiB) Any positive integer Limit in bytes

Raise this if you receive large monorepo push payloads. Lower it to reduce memory pressure on high-traffic gateways.

docs.title: Supported File Formats
docs.text: varTrack auto-detects the format of your config file from its extension. All formats are parsed into the same flat { "key": "value" } map, which is what is validated and what most sinks write. Sinks that store a file as one document (MongoDB and S3 with update_strategy: "STRATEGY_DOCUMENT" or "STRATEGY_FILE") also keep the shape the file parsed to: nested for YAML, JSON, TOML, INI, HCL and XML, flat for .env.

docs.title: Supported formats
docs.text:
Extension Format Notes .yaml, .yml YAML Nested keys flattened with dot notation .json JSON Nested keys flattened with dot notation .toml TOML Sections become key prefixes .env dotenv / KEY=VALUE One KEY=value per line .ini INI Section + key become section.key .hcl HCL Terraform-style config files .xml XML Elements become dot-separated keys

Use --format on the vt sync command to override auto-detection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
YAMLJSON.envTOMLINIHCL 
# configs/app.yaml
database:
  host: mongo.prod.internal
  port: 27017
  name: myapp

feature_flags:
  dark_mode: true
  beta_ui: false

max_connections: 50

Flattened result:

database.port         = "27017"
database.name         = "myapp"
feature_flags.dark_mode = "true"
feature_flags.beta_ui   = "false"
max_connections         = "50"

{
  "database": {
    "host": "mongo.prod.internal",
    "port": 27017
  },
  "max_connections": 50
}

Flattened result:

database.port    = "27017"
max_connections  = "50"

# configs/app.env

DATABASE_PORT=27017
MAX_CONNECTIONS=50
FEATURE_DARK_MODE=true

Flattened result (keys preserved as-is):

DATABASE_HOST       = "mongo.prod.internal"
DATABASE_PORT       = "27017"
MAX_CONNECTIONS     = "50"
FEATURE_DARK_MODE   = "true"

[database]
host = "mongo.prod.internal"
port = 27017

[feature_flags]
dark_mode = true

Flattened result:

database.port          = "27017"
feature_flags.dark_mode = "true"

[database]
host = mongo.prod.internal
port = 27017

[app]

Flattened result:

docs.title: Root key slicing
docs.text:
If your config file uses a vartrack top-level key, varTrack extracts only that subtree:

# Other top-level keys are ignored
app_name: my-service
version: 2.3.1

vartrack:
  database_host: mongo.prod.internal
  max_connections: 50

Only database_host and max_connections are written. This lets you keep varTrack config alongside other metadata in the same file.

docs.title: Dry-run — preview what would be written
docs.text:
Before any real sync, you can simulate the full parse → flatten → env-slice pipeline without writing anything to a sink:

# CLI
vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env staging --dry-run

# HTTP
POST /v1/webhooks/mongo/dry-run

The response shows the exact flat key/value map that would be written — after root_key extraction, env-slicing, and @secret masking. Nothing touches the datasource.

This is especially useful when introducing a new file format or env pattern: run dry-run first to confirm varTrack is parsing and slicing the file exactly as expected before merging to main.

docs.title: Environment key patterns
docs.text: varTrack auto-detects three patterns for environment-keyed config files. No rule config is needed — the structure is inferred automatically.

docs.title: Pattern 1 — all top-level keys are env names
docs.text:
Every top-level value is a dict. varTrack merges default first, then applies the matching env as an override.

# configs/app.yaml
production:
  database_host: mongo.prod.internal
  max_connections: 100
  log_level: warn

staging:
  database_host: mongo.staging.internal
  max_connections: 10
  log_level: info

default:
  max_connections: 5      # fallback for any unknown env
  log_level: debug
  cache_ttl: 60

Push to main (resolved env = production):

database_host   = "mongo.prod.internal"
max_connections = "100"
log_level       = "warn"
cache_ttl       = "60"           ← inherited from default

Push from PR #42 (env = pr-42, no match → default):

max_connections = "5"
log_level       = "debug"
cache_ttl       = "60"

docs.title: Pattern 2 — per-field env sub-keys mixed with scalars
docs.text:
Each field that varies per env has a dict of env → value. Fields that are the same across all envs are plain scalars — they are written as-is for every env.

# configs/app.yaml
database_host:
  production: mongo.prod.internal
  staging:    mongo.staging.internal
  default:    mongo.local

max_connections: 50        # same for every env
log_level: info            # same for every env
cache_ttl:
  production: 300
  staging:    60
  default:    10

Push to main (env = production):

database_host   = "mongo.prod.internal"
max_connections = "50"
log_level       = "info"
cache_ttl       = "300"

Push to develop (env = staging):

database_host   = "mongo.staging.internal"
max_connections = "50"
log_level       = "info"
cache_ttl       = "60"

docs.title: Pattern 3 — env dicts and scalar defaults at the same level
docs.text:
Some keys at the same nesting level are env names (dicts with overrides), others are plain scalars that apply to every env. Order in the file doesn't matter — varTrack categorizes by value type, not position. The env dict is merged on top of the scalars.

{
  "production": { "database_host": "mongo.prod.internal", "log_level": "warn"  },
  "staging":    { "database_host": "mongo.stg.internal",  "log_level": "info"  },
  "default":    { "database_host": "mongo.local",         "log_level": "debug" },
  "max_connections": 50,
  "cache_ttl":       60,
  "app_name":        "my-service"
}

Push to main (env = production):

database_host   = "mongo.prod.internal"   ← from production dict
log_level       = "warn"                  ← from production dict
max_connections = "50"                    ← from scalar
cache_ttl       = "60"                    ← from scalar
app_name        = "my-service"            ← from scalar

Push from PR #42 (env = pr-42, no match → default dict):

database_host   = "mongo.local"
log_level       = "debug"
max_connections = "50"
cache_ttl       = "60"
app_name        = "my-service"

If there is no default dict and no matching env dict, data is returned unchanged.

docs.title: Combining patterns with root_key
docs.text:
All three patterns work after root_key extraction. This lets you embed varTrack config inside files owned by other tools:

# package.json style — but in YAML for readability
name: my-app
version: 1.0.0

vartrack:
  production: { API_URL: "https://api.prod.com", LOG_LEVEL: warn  }
  staging:    { API_URL: "https://api.stg.com",  LOG_LEVEL: info  }
  default:    { API_URL: "https://api.local.com", LOG_LEVEL: debug }
  TIMEOUT: 30

rules: [{
  file_name: "config.yaml"
  root_key:  "vartrack"      // extract the vartrack block first, then detect pattern
  branch_map: { main: "production", develop: "staging" }
}]

Push to main → extracts vartrack subtree → detects Pattern 3 → writes API_URL=https://api.prod.com, LOG_LEVEL=warn, TIMEOUT=30.

docs.title: Per-Repo Overrides (vartrack.json)
docs.text: Individual repositories can override a subset of their central rule configuration without touching config.cue. Place a vartrack.json file at the root of the repository and varTrack will apply its settings on top of the matching rule whenever a webhook is received — the third of the layers a rule is built from.

docs.title: Where the file lives
docs.text:
varTrack reads the first of these it finds at the pushed ref:

  1. vartrack.json
  2. .github/vartrack.json
  3. .gitea/vartrack.json
  4. .gitlab/vartrack.json

The file is read at the pushed commit, so each branch can carry its own — main and develop can override differently.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When a push webhook arrives, the ETL pipeline:

  1. Resolves the rule: the one in config.cue, with the tenant's bundle.json rule laid over it (Stage 1 — Payload)
  2. Fetches vartrack.json from the repository at the pushed commit ref, and resolves the presets it extends
  3. Merges the overridable keys from vartrack.json into the rule: branch_map, file_path_map, variables_map and prune key by key, the others replaced
  4. Applies the config.cue rule's force keys, which win over vartrack.json
  5. Runs ETL and Sync with the merged settings (Stages 2 and 3)

If vartrack.json is absent or empty, the central rule is used unchanged. If it is there but cannot be used — not valid JSON, not a JSON object, or extending a preset that cannot be read — the sync fails with that error: it does not go ahead without settings the repository asked for, such as a dry_run. The schema registry is never affected by per-repo overrides.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "root_key": "app_config",
  "branch_map": {
    "main": "production",
    "staging": "staging",
    "develop": "develop"
  },
  "prune": true,
  "sync_mode": "GIT_UPSERT_ALL"
}

Shared settings can come from presets — here a preset in the org's presets repository, then a key of the repository's own:

{
  "extends": ["local>my-org/presets//repos/checkout"],
  "prune": {"protection": ["experiments.*"]}
}

Place this file at the root of the repository (next to your config file):

my-repo/
├── vartrack.json        ← per-repo overrides
└── configs/
    └── app.yaml         ← your config file (watched by the central rule)

docs.title: Overridable keys
docs.text:
These keys can be set in vartrack.json to override the central rule:

Key Type Description root_key string Subtree to extract before flattening. "" processes the whole file. file_name string Config file path to watch instead of the centrally configured one. file_path_map object Map of env → file_path for per-environment file selection. Merged like branch_map. branch_map object Map of branch → env label. Merged into the central branch mapping; a branch set here wins. branch_as_env bool Use branch name as the environment label. pr_as_env bool Use pr-{number} as the environment label. tag_as_env bool Use tag name as the environment label. sync_mode string AUTO, GIT_UPSERT_ALL, GIT_SMART_REPAIR, or LIVE_STATE. prune bool or object Delete keys from the datasource that are no longer present in Git. An object ({enabled, last, dry_run, protection}) is merged with the rule's; its protection patterns are added to the rule's, never replace them. strict_validation bool Fail the sync if CUE schema validation fails (instead of warn). variables_map object Key-value pairs injected or overridden after ETL transform. Merged like branch_map. dry_run bool Permanently shadow this repo — Stage 3 never writes anything.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
Infrastructure and security-critical keys are always taken from the central bundle and cannot be changed by the repository:

  • platform, datasource, repo_url, tenant_id
  • token, secret_manager, secret_managers
  • repositories, exclude_repositories
  • self_heal and all Celery wiring keys

Any key in vartrack.json that is not in the overridable list above is silently ignored and logged at INFO level.

A key the config.cue rule lists under force cannot be overridden either: force is applied after vartrack.json. For example, force: {prune: {enabled: false}} keeps a production rule from pruning whatever a repository asks for.

docs.title: Interaction with the schema registry
docs.text: vartrack.json has no effect on CUE schema validation. The schema used to validate your config file is always sourced from the tenant's schema registry (configured in config.cue under schema_registry). Per-repo overrides cannot change which schema is applied or bypass validation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Override not applied — Check the orchestrator logs for: 

repo_overrides: no vartrack.json repo=... ref=...
This means the file was not found at the repo root for that commit ref.

Keys ignored — If you see: 

repo_overrides: ignoring non-overridable keys ['platform', ...] repo=...
Those keys are infrastructure-level and cannot be overridden from the repo.

Preset not found — A preset in extends that cannot be read fails the sync with: 

vartrack.json in https://...: preset local>my-org/presets:nope: no nope.json at main in my-org/presets

Invalid JSON — A parse error fails the sync with: 

vartrack.json in https://... is not valid JSON: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 3 column 5 (char 41)
Fix the file and push again; the sync runs with it.

docs.title: Schema Registry
docs.text:
The schema registry is a Git repository that holds two things:

  1. CUE schema files — used to validate config files before any write
  2. bundle.json / rules.json — the tenant's layer of rule settings, laid over the rules in config.cue (see How a rule is built)

docs.title: Repo structure
docs.text:
my-org/schemas/                  ← schema registry repo
├── bundle.json                  ← the tenant's rule settings (optional)
├── app-settings.yaml.cue        ← CUE schema for app-settings.yaml
├── config.toml.cue              ← CUE schema for config.toml
├── dotenv.cue                   ← CUE schema for .env files
└── default.cue                  ← fallback schema when no file-specific match

The schema repo is pointed to from config.cue:

schema_registry: {
  platform: "github"
  repo:     "my-org/schemas"
  branch:   "main"
}

varTrack clones this repo for each tenant on first use and refreshes it automatically on a TTL (default 5 minutes) or immediately when the schema repo itself receives a push webhook.

docs.title: How a rule is built
docs.text:
varTrack builds the rule a sync runs with in layers: the admin's config, the tenant's config and the repository's own. Each layer overrides the one before it, key by key:

# Layer Where 1 The rule in config.cue the bundle every service reads 2 The tenant's rule bundle.json in the tenant's schema repo — optional 3 The repository's overrides vartrack.json in the pushed repo — optional (Per-Repo Overrides) 4 force the config.cue rule's force block

branch_map, file_path_map, variables_map and prune are merged key by key across layers: a branch_map of {develop: staging} in bundle.json adds to the {main: production} of config.cue. The prune.protection patterns of every layer add up — a layer can protect more keys, never fewer. Every other key is replaced.

bundle.json and vartrack.json can also pull in shared settings with extends — see Presets.

Keys only config.cue sets. These are dropped from bundle.json with a warning (… sets mongo_uri, self_heal, which only config.cue sets — ignored). The gateway routes pushes by config.cue's repositories and the watcher heals the rules config.cue marks self_heal, so another value further down would split the services:

  • the datasource's connection settings and credentials: every sink key a datasource block sets (mongo_uri, database, collection, update_strategy, redis_hosts, s3_bucket, ssh_host, …)
  • the rule's secret_manager, repositories, exclude_repositories, overrides, self_heal, force and tenants

force cannot pin these either; they are set on the rule itself.

Which rules exist. The rules are config.cue's, since the gateway only routes pushes to those. A bundle.json rule for a platform and datasource with no rule in config.cue is ignored with a warning. A config.cue rule that no tenant's bundle.json names still syncs, as tenant default's. Its repo_url is derived from the platform's endpoint and the rule's only repository (http://gitea:3000 + acme/configs → http://gitea:3000/acme/configs.git); a webhook for a rule covering several repositories reads the pushed one.

A bundle whose config.cue has no rules gets only the second layer: bundle.json's rules are used as they are, and a datasource's config.cue settings still win over the same keys in a rule.

docs.title: Presets (extends)
docs.text:
A preset is a JSON file of rule settings in a Git repository, shared by every bundle.json or vartrack.json that names it in extends. A presets repository might hold:

my-org/presets/
├── default.json        ← {"prune": {"protection": ["_vt_*"]}}
├── production.json     ← {"extends": ["local>my-org/presets"], "prune": {"protection": ["manual.*"]}}
└── repos/
    └── checkout.json   ← {"prune": {"protection": ["features.*"]}}

A preset is named like this:

extends entry File local>my-org/presets default.json in my-org/presets local>my-org/presets:production production.json local>my-org/presets//repos/checkout repos/checkout.json local>my-org/presets:production#v2 production.json on branch or tag v2 (default: main) gitea>my-org/presets:production the same file on config.cue's platform gitea (any platform name: github, gitea-team, …), read with that platform's token

local> (or no prefix) is the Git server of the file naming the preset: the schema repo's for bundle.json, the pushed repo's for vartrack.json, and the preset's own inside a preset.

How presets are resolved:

  • presets are merged left to right, then the settings beside extends go on top;
  • a preset can extend presets itself; one already in the chain is skipped;
  • a preset's description is dropped;
  • a preset that cannot be read, or is not a JSON object, is an error: a tenant whose bundle.json names one has no rules until it is fixed (logged as bundle.json cannot be used — the tenant has no rules until it is fixed: …), and a sync whose vartrack.json names one fails.

The same holds for a bundle.json that does not parse: the tenant does not fall back to the config.cue rules without its layer.

A preset adds to its layer only: presets that a bundle.json extends are part of the tenant's layer, so keys only config.cue sets are dropped from them too, and presets that a vartrack.json extends are limited to its overridable keys. A changed preset is picked up when the tenant's schema repo is next refreshed (every SCHEMA_TTL_SECONDS, or on a push to it); a vartrack.json's presets are read on every sync.

docs.title: bundle.json
docs.text: bundle.json is a JSON array of rule objects — one entry per platform + datasource the tenant syncs. Each entry holds only what the tenant adds to, or changes in, the config.cue rule for that platform and datasource.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Two formats are accepted:

Array (recommended): 

[
  { ... rule object ... },
  { ... rule object ... }
]

Object with a rules key — which can also extends presets for every rule in it: 

{
  "extends": ["local>my-org/presets:production"],
  "rules": [
    { ... rule object ... }
  ]
}

A rule can extends presets of its own as well; they come after the file's.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With this rule in config.cue:

rules: [{
  platform:     "github"
  datasource:   "mongo"
  repositories: ["acme/app-configs"]
  file_name:    "configs/app.yaml"
  branch_map:   {main: "production"}
  self_heal:    true
  force:        {prune: {enabled: false}}   // production never prunes
}]

the tenant's bundle.json adds a staging branch, a root key and the smart-repair sync mode:

[
  {
    "platform":   "github",
    "datasource": "mongo",
    "tenant_id":  "acme",
    "branch_map": {"develop": "staging"},
    "root_key":   "vartrack",
    "sync_mode":  "GIT_SMART_REPAIR",
    "prune":      true
  }
]
